performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
question: How can two melodies at different speeds stand for two people?
intro: Two men, one rich and imposing, one poor and nervous, are drawn as two tunes that finally sound at once. Hear which one commands and which one pleads. Instruments named here follow Ravel’s orchestration, the probable but undocumented version.

sections.label: Both themes together
sections.mNote: Goldenberg returns above Schmuÿle’s repeated notes

cues.title: A slow, gruff unison
cues.text: Goldenberg is drawn as a slow melody played in unison by lower woodwinds and strings, with few attacks (often under one a second) at a strong level. It leans on the augmented second, a wide step in the scale.
cues.evidence: Gruff unison in lower woodwinds and strings: Philharmonia guide; slow unison stressing the augmented second: Peter Laki’s Cleveland Orchestra note. Onsets per second 1.2, 0.8, 0.6, 0.2, 0.6, 0.2 at 0:00–0:25; relative level −14.8 to −9.1 dB.

cues.title: The poor man’s repeated notes
cues.text: Right at about 0:39 the colour flips: Schmuÿle’s theme enters as quick repeated notes on a muted trumpet over woodwind chords. Detected attacks leap to five a second and the brightness doubles.
cues.evidence: Spectral brightness rises from 1,282 Hz (0:35) to 2,515 Hz (0:40) and onsets from 1.0 to 4.8 per second; a 1-second pass puts the jump at 0:38–0:40. Strongest boundary at 0:40 (novelty 1.00). Muted trumpet and woodwind chords: Philharmonia guide; “repeated notes seem to choke up”: Laki’s note.

cues.title: Two drawings Mussorgsky owned
cues.text: Hartmann drew “A rich Jew wearing a fur hat” and “A poor Jew: Sandomierz” on a month’s stay in Poland in 1868, and Mussorgsky owned both. They are the portraits behind this movement.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note (https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition) for the two drawings and Sandomierz in 1868; Wikipedia’s article (movement 6) for Mussorgsky owning the pictures and the movement’s portraits. When the names Goldenberg and Schmuÿle were first written is left out because the cited sources disagree. Related edge: hartmann-pictures--mussorgsky-pictures-1874. The note sits in a steady passage (−18 to −19 dB, 0:45–1:05).

cues.title: Both men at once
cues.text: At about 1:09 the level jumps by some six decibels as Goldenberg’s theme returns while Schmuÿle’s quick notes carry on. Ravel gives Goldenberg to the whole string section and Schmuÿle to one muted trumpet.
cues.evidence: Relative level −19.5 dB (1:05) to −11.7 dB (1:10); boundary at 1:06 (novelty 0.89); a 1-second pass puts the jump at about 1:09 (−15.7 to −9.1 dB) with attacks still near five a second. Form A–B–A+B: Wikipedia; strings and single muted trumpet: Laki’s note.

cues.title: A missing Promenade
cues.text: Mussorgsky follows this picture with a fifth Promenade, a near repeat of the opening. Ravel leaves it out, so this recording goes straight on to Limoges. Many orchestral versions of the suite omit it.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article (the fifth Promenade; arrangements: Ravel omitted the Promenade between Goldenberg and Limoges). The Cleveland Orchestra note’s movement list shows the same omission. Fits this Skidmore album: four Promenades and no fifth. The note sits in the steady, loud stretch where both themes sound (−11 to −14 dB, 1:10–1:35).

cues.title: The quarrel stops
cues.text: At about 1:41 the level drops by roughly fifteen decibels and the quick notes cease. The remaining twenty-five seconds are slow and quiet, with fewer than two attacks a second for most of the time.
cues.evidence: Strongest late boundary at 1:42 (novelty 0.99); a 2-second pass gives −9.8 dB at 1:40 and −25.1 dB at 1:42, with onsets per second falling from 5.0 to 0.2 at 1:45. Onsets 0.2, 0.8, 0.4, 1.4, 1.0 at 1:45–2:05.

cues.title: A sudden dismissal
cues.text: At about 2:06 a loud chord breaks a hush, the level jumping from about −26 dB to −7 dB. Steinberg notes that Ravel has Goldenberg dismiss Schmuÿle more abruptly than Mussorgsky’s long final note does.
cues.evidence: A 2-second pass gives −26.1 dB at 2:04 and −7.0 dB at 2:06, with brightness rising from 914 Hz to 1,677 Hz; the report shows −23.6 dB at 2:00 and −15.0 dB at 2:05. Ravel’s more abrupt ending: Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note.

transitions.title: A slow march gives way to nerves
transitions.how: Goldenberg’s slow, heavy theme dies away to a few quiet notes, and Schmuÿle’s theme starts abruptly: much faster repeated notes, high and thin, with woodwind chords beneath. The score’s tempo mark changes from Andante to Andantino. Mussorgsky contrasts the two men by speed, register, brightness and the number of notes per second, and the join is a cut, not a transition.
transitions.evidence: Strongest boundary at 0:40 (novelty 1.00); brightness 1,282 Hz (0:35) to 2,515 Hz (0:40); onsets per second 1.0 to 4.8; a 1-second pass puts the jump at 0:38–0:40. Tempo marks Andante, grave-energico and Andantino: Lamm’s score (Mutopia, two-jews.ly).

transitions.title: The rich man’s theme returns above him
transitions.how: After a passage at a steady, quiet level, Goldenberg’s slow theme returns at full volume while Schmuÿle’s quick repeated notes carry on. The two themes are now superimposed: the ternary form A–B–A+B brings the contrasting ideas together, so the rich man’s weight overpowers the poor man’s nervous patter without silencing it. The join is a change of volume and texture, not of key.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 1:06 (novelty 0.89); relative level −19.5 dB (1:05) to −11.7 dB (1:10); onsets per second stay at 4.4–5.0 from 1:05 to 1:35; the superimposed form is from Wikipedia’s description and Laki’s note.

transitions.title: The quick notes cut out
transitions.how: The superimposed themes stop together at about 1:41, with a fall of some fifteen decibels. What follows is slow and quiet, with few attacks, and it ends with one loud chord. In Ravel’s version Goldenberg dismisses Schmuÿle sooner than in Mussorgsky’s piano original, which ends on a long note.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 1:42 (novelty 0.99); a 2-second pass gives −9.8 dB at 1:40, −25.1 dB at 1:42; onsets 5.0 per second (1:35) to 0.2 (1:45); final chord at about 2:06. Ravel’s abrupt ending: Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (2:10; this file is 2:08), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
